approach_variants.name: Shannon Ridge Trail #742 (standard)
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Baker Lake Road (FR 11) north from SR 20 near milepost 82, then FR 1152, then the 1152-014 spur to its end. The spur is rough and rutted; high clearance is the sensible minimum. An overnight in the park needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, obtained in person at Marblemount or arranged in advance with the wilderness office.

The trail opens as an old roadbed running northeast. It stays easy for roughly the first two miles, then a long-standing blowdown belt makes for tedious weaving before the tread turns into a real trail and angles left through brush onto the open crest of Shannon Ridge.

Above treeline the ridge rolls along through meadow and scattered timber to a pass at about 5,400 ft, where a major north-south ridge is joined and the Sulphide Glacier with the summit pyramid behind it comes into view for the first time. One party logged roughly four and a half hours and about 2,800 ft of gain to this point. Camps are established on the glacier's lower flats at about 6,200 ft and higher at about 6,500 ft; both have had composting toilets, but the upper one has been closed when full, so carry blue bags. There is no reliable running water above timberline late in the season.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts where the glacier ends against the summit pyramid, and the whole navigational problem is picking the right groove out of several parallel ones. Walk the glacier to its high point directly beneath the CENTRE of the rock pyramid — not around either shoulder. The correct line is the central gully: it is the one carrying fixed rappel anchors and old slings, because every party that summits rappels back down it, and its rock is scoured and boot-polished rather than mossy. If you are looking up a steep parallel groove with no anchors visible and clean-cut, untravelled rock, you are one gully off; traverse back toward the middle of the face.

The last few metres before rock are the giveaway that you have arrived: a short steep snow patch and then a moat where the glacier has pulled back from the pyramid. Early in the season a snow bridge spans it; by August it is an open gap you step or scramble across, and that step is the true start of the climbing. If you are still walking on flat glacier with rock only in the distance, you are short of it.

A second, separate option exists — a gully on the southwest side, reached by continuing around the western edge of the glacier until the pyramid stands squarely in front of you. It is a distinct line, not a variation of the central gully, and parties who take it still descend the central one.
hazards: loose rock funnelled down the summit-pyramid gully, worst late season when the snow has melted out of it
moat between glacier and pyramid, which widens through the season
crevasses on the Sulphide as snow bridges thin after midsummer
blowdown belt on the lower trail is easy to lose in the dark
no reliable water above timberline

approach_variants.name: Lake Ann Trail #600 from SR 542
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Lake Ann trailhead on the east side of the Mount Baker Highway, roughly a mile below Artist Point. The trail goes DOWN first — several hundred feet over its first mile and a half — before climbing back to the broad saddle above Lake Ann at roughly four miles.

Just past the saddle there is an unsigned fork. The right branch drops to the lake, the campsites and the outlet, which is the last easy water. The left branch is the climbers' boot path, and it is distinct and well trodden — a very obvious break heading east toward the mountain.

That path sidehills north beneath Shuksan's lower moraines, switchbacking and crossing two gullies over talus and lingering snow tongues, and becomes vague right where you need it most: just short of the first chimney. Parties typically reckon around six hours from the car to the high camp on or above the chimneys, and expect the snow tongues to be firm enough for microspikes and an axe in the early morning well into July.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the crux of the whole approach and it is regularly got wrong. Where the boot path fades, stop and look EAST at the cliff band. You want a small snowfield pushed up against the base of the cliff, with a right-slanting ramp of slope at its foot and, almost straight across from you, a deep green gully. Drop about fifty feet and cross straight over the talus and snow — usually there is an obvious boot pack — until you are at the cliffs.

The test that settles it: the correct gully has a beaten dirt TRAIL running up it and rock scoured clean by thousands of boots, and at its foot there is a rappel station slung around a tangle of dead tree roots. Look for the trail, not for a plausible line of weakness.

The negative markers are unambiguous. If you are looking up a gully whose rock is furred with moss or lichen, it is the wrong one. If you are climbing on heather with no path underfoot at any point on this route, you are off it. And there are tempting side paths that lead out to cliff-edge viewpoints and stop — if the ground ahead simply ends at a drop, reverse and find the trail again rather than pressing on. The chimneys are a braided ledge-and-step system, so it is also easy to overshoot the entrance entirely and end up traversing along the base of the cliff band past it; if the cliff on your right has become continuous with no green break in it, you have gone too far.
hazards: rockfall inside the chimneys, especially with parties above
firm or icy snow tongues on the talus traverse before the sun hits
the route-finding itself — the boot path deliberately goes obscure right at the chimney entrance
several dead-end side paths ending at cliff edges

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Lodge road (standard)
approach_variants.season: spring to early summer; needs snow cover
approach_variants.notes:
Pull off at the old White Salmon lodge site on the Mount Baker Highway, walk around the gate, and follow the old road past the lodge for about a mile to where it finishes in an old clearcut.

What you do next depends entirely on snow cover, and getting this wrong is the single biggest time sink on the approach. With GOOD cover, drop northeast off the clearcut down to White Salmon Creek and walk the valley toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier — pleasant going. WITHOUT good cover, do not descend into the valley at all: hold your elevation as you enter the clearcut and contour around instead, giving up height only where a rock band or a stream crossing forces it. The valley bottom without snow is slide alder and devil's club.

From the glacier area, the route continues up toward the shoulder at the foot of the face.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the shoulder at about 5,500 ft on the divide between the White Salmon Glacier and the Price cirque, and it is confirmed by what you can see BEHIND and BELOW you rather than above: from the shoulder you look down onto Price Lake. If Price Lake is not below you, you have not gained the shoulder — you are still on the glacier or on its moraine, and the face above you is foreshortened enough that it will look like the start.

The shoulder has good bivy sites, which is the second confirmation: flat ground here is scarce, so a usable bivy platform at this height on this ridge is the place.

From there the face itself is entered by a gully angling up and to the LEFT onto the North Face. Some parties instead continue up the glacier past the shoulder; if you have passed the bivy ground and are still on continuous glacier, you have gone by the entrance.
hazards: avalanches off the Hanging Glacier, which is very active and sweeps the approach terrain
slide alder and devil's club in the White Salmon valley once the snow has gone
unbridged stream crossings when contouring the low-snow variation
crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier

approach_variants.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
approach_variants.notes: An alternative used mainly by ski parties: start at the base of Chair 8 in the ski area and make a downhill traverse into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley, then climb over four thousand feet up the glacier. It removes the clearcut and the road walk at the cost of a long climb from the valley floor and a committing descent to start the day.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same shoulder at roughly 5,500 ft with Price Lake visible below to the north-west. Coming up from the valley floor rather than contouring in, the trap is stopping at the first flat ground on the glacier's margin — keep going until you are on the divide itself and the ground on the far side falls away toward Price Lake.
hazards: avalanche exposure from the Hanging Glacier across the whole basin
the initial descent commits you to regaining that height on the way out

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Lodge road
approach_variants.notes:
Small pull-off at the old White Salmon lodge on the Mount Baker Highway. Walk around the gate and take the old road past the lodge site for about a mile until it ends at an old clearcut.

With good snow, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the glacier. Without good snow, do NOT go down into the valley — hold your height entering the clearcut and contour, shedding elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings. This is the same decision that governs the North Face approach, and it is the difference between a walk and a fight with slide alder.

Note that the record on file for this route describes going south past Lake Ann and over Austin Pass. That is not the way parties reach the White Salmon Glacier; the drainage is entered from the White Salmon side of the highway.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route proper begins at the foot of the White Salmon Glacier, or from the bivy sites up and right of it. Ascend the glacier weaving between rock outcrops and crevasses; the marker you are climbing toward is the base of Winnie's Slide at roughly 6,800 ft. Winnie's Slide is unmistakable once you are under it — the angle jumps to around forty to forty-five degrees for a few hundred feet, and it is the only thing on this side of the mountain that steepens like that. Above it you step onto the Upper Curtis Glacier.

If you are still on low-angle glacier threading around rock islands, you are below the slide, however long you have been walking. Conversely, if you have topped out on flatter glacier without a steep pitch behind you, you have drifted off the line and are somewhere else on the White Salmon.
hazards: avalanche off the Hanging Glacier across the approach basin
brush in the valley bottom without snow cover
crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier
Winnie's Slide holds firm ice when it has melted back

approach_variants.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
approach_variants.notes: From the base of Chair 8, traverse downhill into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley and then climb over four thousand feet to near the base of Hell's Highway at the top of the glacier. This is the ski-descent party's usual line in.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Winnie's Slide at about 6,800 ft is still the reference feature low on the route; higher, the head of the White Salmon is marked by the base of Hell's Highway. Neither is a subtle feature — both are abrupt steepenings out of low-angle glacier.
hazards: a committing descent at the start that must be reclimbed on the way out
Hanging Glacier avalanche debris across the valley

approach_variants.name: Nooksack Cirque Trail #750 via Ruth Creek Road
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; heavy early-season snowpack often preferred
approach_variants.notes:
Ruth Creek Road (FS-32) off the Mount Baker Highway near the Hannegan Pass Road junction. There is no bridge over Ruth Creek at the trailhead — the crossing is on a large logjam a little downstream, and in high water or after rain it has turned parties around before they started.

Beyond the crossing the old roadbed runs about two miles through old growth to the original trailhead, then it is river-bottom travel along the North Fork Nooksack: gravel bars when the water is low, riparian brush when it is not. You pass the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary at roughly three miles and the national park boundary at about four.

Rather than continuing into the cirque, leave the tread and watch ACROSS the valley for the steep drainage of Price Creek. Cross the Nooksack on a log and climb the forested hillside toward Price Lake — steep, open forest with old flagging, about an hour and a half from the river to the lake basin at roughly 4,700 ft. Budget the better part of a day for the approach; most parties treat the whole climb as two to three days.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two candidate stopping points and they are not the same place. From the moraine below Price Lake, work up through the cliff bands onto the heathery ridge on the lake's SOUTH side, then ascend the rock slabs up and to the RIGHT. The first bivy sites are flat granite just below the ridge crest at the glacier's margin, around 6,000-6,500 ft — that is a camp, not the start of the route.

The start of the climbing is the exposed snow saddle beneath Nooksack Tower, roughly an hour further along the glacier. You get there by gaining the glacier at the ridge crest and traversing climber's right. You will know you are there because Nooksack Tower's mass is directly above you and the gully between the tower and the main lobe of the Price is the thing you are trying to get past — it is the rockfall funnel, and it has delivered blocks the size of a television down onto the traverse.

If you are still on heather and slabs above Price Lake with no glacier underfoot, you are below the start. If you are on flat granite with a view down to the lake, you are at the bivy, not the saddle.
hazards: unbridged Ruth Creek log crossing, sometimes impassable
brush and vague route-finding along the river flats
steep, loose, unofficial climbers' path to Price Lake
rockfall and icefall down the gully between Nooksack Tower and the glacier's main lobe — large blocks reported

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trail #677 to the Hogsback
approach_variants.notes:
Glacier Creek Road (FS 39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead. Trail 677 switchbacks up through old growth and avalanche chutes, crossing Grouse, Kulshan and Heliotrope Creeks. Those crossings are fed by glacier melt and run highest in the afternoon, so cross early on the way in and expect them to be worse coming out.

At roughly two and a quarter miles the trail forks: left continues to the Coleman Glacier overlook, right is the climbers' path onto the moraine crest known as the Hogsback. Standard camp sits at about 6,000 ft, around two and a half miles and 2,800 ft above the car. There is running water up to about the old Kulshan Cabin site; above the camp there is nothing but what you melt. Some parties camp higher, toward the Black Buttes at around 7,200 ft.

Glacier Creek Road has a history of washing out; when it has been closed low, parties have added several miles of road on foot or bike before reaching the sign-in kiosk.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing begins where the Hogsback's crest gives out and you step onto the Coleman — rope up when the snow slope steepens rather than at a fixed altitude, because the transition moves with the snowline.

The feature that actually matters for navigation is the saddle between Colfax Peak and Baker's summit cone. From the top of the moraine head roughly east up the glacier, curving south as the crevasses dictate, staying near the Colfax ridge but not under it — that flank avalanches every year and has left debris blocks as big as cars strewn across the track. When you reach the saddle, turn left, east and slightly north, and go up the pumice ridge that leads to the foot of the Roman Wall.

The negative marker is the one that catches people in cloud: if you are climbing steepening snow with rock close on one side and you have NOT passed through a broad, obvious col, you are on the flank below Colfax, not on the Roman Wall. The Roman Wall is approached across open ground with the saddle behind you and nothing beside you. This stretch has almost no natural handrails, the summit plateau on top is very large and flat, and parties get lost here in whiteout more than anywhere else on the mountain — wand it on the way up.
hazards: creek crossings surge with afternoon glacial melt
annual avalanche debris off the Colfax Peak ridge across the standard track
crevasses on the Coleman and upper Deming
whiteout navigation on the featureless upper glacier and summit plateau
no water above the Hogsback camp

approach_variants.name: Park Butte Trail 603 and the Railroad Grade to Sandy Camp
approach_variants.notes:
Schriebers Meadow / Park Butte trailhead at about 3,400 ft, at the end of the Sulphur Creek road. Cross Sulphur Creek near the start — bridged or on logs, but a genuine ford during peak snowmelt — then climb through the meadow and forest switchbacks.

At about two and a quarter miles a SIGNED junction sends you right onto the Railroad Grade Trail 603.2. Stone steps take you up onto the crest of the lateral moraine. There are three established camp areas along the way; Sandy Camp at about 5,900 ft is the usual one for climbing, roughly four miles in with 2,600 ft of gain.

Above Morovitz Meadows there is no reliable water other than melted snow.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are at the start when the moraine crest simply runs out. The Railroad Grade tapers off just before 6,000 ft into the sandy flats and rock-walled tent platforms of Sandy Camp; that is where the trail stops being a trail and where parties rope up for the glacier.

The simplest confirmation on the way up is which side the ice is on: walking the moraine crest toward the mountain, the Easton Glacier drops away on your RIGHT the entire way. If the glacier is on your left, or if there is no glacier beside you at all, you never took the signed junction and are still on the Park Butte trail heading for the lookout.

Higher, the feature that tells you the glacier is done is Sherman Crater — steaming, sulphurous ground at the head of the ice. The Roman Wall is the steep snow rising beyond it, and the true summit is a short traverse past the top of the wall. Smelling sulphur means you are at the TOP of the glacier and should be turning up onto the wall, not continuing toward the crater.
hazards: Sulphur Creek crossing during peak melt
exposed, loose moraine crest in wind
crevasses on the broad Easton, worse late season
volcanic gas and unstable ground at Sherman Crater
no water above Morovitz Meadows

approach_variants.name: Scott Paul Trail to Crag View
approach_variants.notes:
Same parking as the Easton route, at Schriebers Meadow. The Scott Paul Trail branches off within about a hundred feet of the trailhead and contours around the base of the mountain through forest, meadow and moraine.

After a few miles an UNMARKED junction sends the route north onto a steep climbers' path. That path leads to Crag View camp at about 6,500 ft, roughly three and a half miles in with 3,300 ft of gain. The Squak Glacier is gained near Point 6513, which some maps label Crag View.

This is the early-season choice on Baker's south side; later in the year a bergschrund develops on the route that is awkward to get past. Higher up the route merges with the Easton line near Sherman Crater.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Two separate things to find, and the first one is the one people miss. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail at about 4,600 ft, very shortly after you reach the first open meadow with views out to Baker and Shuksan. There is no sign. If you are still walking graded tread that contours AROUND the mountain rather than climbing toward it, you have walked past the junction — the correct path goes up.

The second is the top of the ridge. Crag View is the end of the line for walking: the last hundred feet or so of the ridge narrow to a class 3 scramble with serious exposure in places, and the glacier is stepped onto near Point 6513 at the top of that. If the crest you are on still has a comfortable walking path, you are below Crag View — the change from path to scramble IS the marker.
hazards: unmarked trail junction at about 4,600 ft, easily walked past
exposed class 3 finish on the ridge to Crag View
bergschrund on the Squak that becomes difficult later in the season
volcanic gas near Sherman Crater where the route joins the Easton

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman Glacier crossing
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to Coleman-Deming as far as camp: Glacier Creek Road to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, Trail 677 through old growth to the fork at about two and a quarter miles, then the moraine crest to the Hogsback camps at around 6,000 ft — two and a half miles and 2,800 ft, four to five hours with a heavy pack. There are dry pitches at the top of the Hogsback.

From camp the two routes part company. The North Ridge crosses the Coleman toward the toe of the ridge, threading between hundred-foot seracs and large open crevasses. This crossing changes year to year and is genuine route-finding, not a bootpack — and because this route sees far less traffic than Coleman-Deming, there may be no track and no established bridges to follow.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The toe of the ridge is guarded by a DOUBLE bergschrund, and that pair of cracks is the thing to look for — it is the standard start and it is what tells you that you have arrived rather than stopped early on the glacier. Probe as you approach: parties have found a third, hidden crevasse tucked between the two obvious ones.

Above the schrunds the standard line goes up a broad snow gully of about forty degrees to gain the crest. Confirm before committing: the ground above should narrow into a defined snow-and-ice crest, and the enormous ice cliff that spans the north face should be overhead higher up. That ice cliff is the route's crux and its base is guarded by a big crevasse most parties turn on the left.

The usual error is being drawn onward by the boot track that keeps going up-glacier toward the Coleman-Deming col. If the ground ahead of you is broad open glacier trending toward a saddle, you have walked past the ridge. If the schrund is impassable or the snow is bottomless, parties have traversed hard toward the rock bands, on the reasoning that there are no crevasses in rock — but that is a fallback, not the route.
hazards: double bergschrund with a reported hidden third crevasse between the two visible ones
serac and crevasse navigation crossing the Coleman with no established track
icefall and rockfall exposure near the ice cliff
the schrund can close the standard start out entirely by late summer
far less traffic than the standard route, so no broken trail

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge to a high Hogsback camp
approach_variants.notes:
Heliotrope Ridge trailhead via Glacier Creek Road. Trail 677 through old growth and avalanche chutes with a couple of unbridged creek crossings, then at about two and a quarter miles take the right-hand climbers' fork off the maintained trail onto the moraine. Past the old Kulshan Cabin site — the last running water — climb the Hogsback crest.

Parties on this route camp higher than the standard Coleman-Deming crowd, commonly around 6,700 ft and sometimes as high as 7,200, either on the ridge itself or on the flats toward the Black Buttes and the Roman Nose. Above camp everything is melted snow.

From camp the line goes up the centre of the broken Coleman. Trip reports consistently describe this as the real crux of the day: weaving round large crevasses, crossing bridges of uncertain quality, and occasionally a committing jump or a short vertical step to get established. It changes materially from season to season.

Starts are early — anything from late evening to half past four in the morning — specifically to be through the exposed glacier and onto the lower headwall before the sun loosens the wall and the Black Buttes above.

Glacier Creek Road has washed out before; when the road is closed low it has added several miles on foot or bike before the kiosk.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base sits at about 8,500 ft, immediately LEFT of the Roman Nose — the rock prow that bounds the headwall on its south side. Use the Roman Nose as the handrail: you want to be tucked under the face just past it, not out in the middle of the glacier.

The positive confirmation is that there is always a bergschrund here, and above it the slope kicks up into sustained forty-five to fifty degree ground that does not lie back again until around 10,200 ft. If the ground above you eases off within a couple of rope lengths, you are not on the headwall.

The negative marker matters because the two features are neighbours: the Coleman Headwall is a broad FACE, and the North Ridge is the defined arete bounding it. If you find yourself at the foot of a narrow crest with a double bergschrund rather than a wide slope, you have gone too far and you are at the North Ridge. Some parties deliberately trend up toward the North Ridge tracks around 8,000 ft to use the broken trail, then drop back down and cut under the Roman Nose — if you are following that plan, the drop back down is not optional.
hazards: the Coleman Glacier crossing itself — large crevasses, questionable bridges, occasionally a barely reversible move
rockfall and icefall off the headwall and the Black Buttes once the sun is on them
bergschrund at the base of the wall every season
no water above camp

approach_variants.name: Artist Point, Ptarmigan Ridge and the Portals
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Mount Baker Highway to its end at Artist Point. Start on Chain Lakes Trail 682 for about a mile to the Ptarmigan Ridge junction, then follow Ptarmigan Ridge Trail 682.1 along the crest. Three miles from that junction the trail reaches the base of Coleman Pinnacle, and half a mile further is Camp Kiser — about five miles in from Artist Point.

The snow on this stretch does not melt out until late in the season, so early parties face a long slog and steep snow chutes, while later parties get easier walking and much harder route-finding as the bootpaths multiply and diverge.

Beyond Camp Kiser the graded tread ends and a bootpath threads the rocky ground of the Portals. From there the route drops onto the Rainbow Glacier, crosses onto the Park Glacier, and heads up toward the headwall with the Cockscomb above it. Most parties camp near the Portals.

Note that the elevation on file for Camp Kiser looks high; sources describe it as a nondescript flat five miles in rather than a high camp on the mountain proper.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Camp Kiser is almost impossible to identify if nobody is camped there — it is an unmarked flat spot, not a named feature you can see. Do not navigate by it. Navigate by Coleman Pinnacle, which the trail passes directly beneath half a mile earlier and which is a genuine landmark; Camp Kiser is the next flat ground after it.

The reliable test for whether you have left the trail system is underfoot: if you can still see graded tread, you have not reached the Portals. The Portals are rock formations and the ground through them is a braid of unofficial bootpaths going in several directions — that confusion IS the marker that you are in the right place, and the general direction is simply to keep gaining the ridge.

Beyond the Portals you must DROP onto the Rainbow Glacier before crossing to the Park. If you are still contouring at height with no glacier below you, you have not committed to the descent yet. The headwall itself is identified from the Park Glacier by the Cockscomb rising directly above it — the headwall is the wall beneath that formation, not any of the other steep ground on the glacier's rim.

Baker's Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers are on the opposite, west and north-west flanks and are never crossed on this approach; if you are on either of them you are on the wrong side of the mountain.
hazards: long steep snow chutes on the approach early in the season
multiplying bootpaths through the Portals once the snow melts
crevasses on the Rainbow and Park Glaciers
Camp Kiser is unmarked and easily walked through

approach_variants.name: Artist Point, Ptarmigan Ridge and the Portals
approach_variants.notes:
The same walk in as the Park Glacier Headwall: Chain Lakes Trail 682 from Artist Point for about a mile to the Ptarmigan Ridge junction, then Trail 682.1 along the crest past Coleman Pinnacle to Camp Kiser at roughly five miles. Past Camp Kiser the maintained trail ends and a primitive bootpath takes over through the Portals.

From there leave the crest on snow, traverse below the ridgeline to a rocky saddle, cross to its far side, work beneath the cliff bands down onto the Rainbow Glacier, cross it and climb onto the Park Glacier. Camps are usually near the Portals.

Snow lingers here into late season, which makes the walk long early and the navigation harder later.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Cockscomb is the formation above the Park Glacier Headwall — the ridge is gained by going up the Park Glacier through the crevasses toward the headwall with the Cockscomb standing above it, then following the ridge to the summit plateau.

Use the Cockscomb itself as the aiming mark rather than any point on the glacier: it is the only thing on this side of the mountain that reads as a serrated rock crest above a headwall. If you are on a glacier with no rock crest above the wall in front of you, you are on the Rainbow rather than the Park and have not finished the crossing.

One durable negative check: the Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers lie on Baker's west and north-west flanks and are not crossed on this approach at any point.
hazards: steep snow chutes and long snow travel early in the season
unmarked bootpath braid through the Portals
crevasses on both the Rainbow and the Park
cliff bands to be turned between the rocky saddle and the Rainbow Glacier

approach_variants.name: Niederprum Trail #653 to Lone Tree Pass and High Pass
approach_variants.season: late Apr-Jun for snow cover; the line goes later but on more rock
approach_variants.notes:
Niederprum trailhead at the end of Old Mine Road above Darrington. The Moose Creek bridge just past the gate has been closed and barricaded for years, so parties park at the gate, get past the barricade on foot and walk the road roughly a mile and a quarter to the real trailhead — extra distance and gain that older guidebook figures do not include.

Trail #653 switchbacks through forest into the Boulder River Wilderness and reaches 'the flat' at about 3,200 ft, a level clearing on the site of an old mining cabin and the natural rest or camp spot. Beyond it the maintained tread ends and a boot path threads thinning, brushy forest with deadfall.

Above that the route traverses south through moderately dense forest between roughly 4,500 and 4,700 ft to reach a broad snow couloir, which is climbed to Lone Tree Pass at about 5,000 ft. From the pass, traverse east along the ridge and then drop several hundred feet southeast to a small lake and flat meadow — a sheltered bivy. A long rising traverse east below cliff bands then leads to a broad gully up to High Pass at about 6,100 ft, and over it onto the So-Bahli-Ahli (Whitehorse) Glacier.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Lone Tree Pass CANNOT be picked out from directly beneath it, and that is the single most useful thing to know about this approach. Look at the mountain from the valley before you start — from the highway at Darrington — and fix where the pass sits relative to the shoulder, because once you are traversing inside the forest between 4,500 and 4,700 ft there is nothing to aim at. The confirmation from inside the trees is the ground itself: you are traversing, not climbing, and the correct entry is where that traversing forest opens into a BROAD snow couloir. A narrow gully or a steep timbered rib is not it.

For the upper half, the landmark is White Benchmark, Point 6357 — a blocky tower that works as a lighthouse for the whole rising traverse to High Pass. Keep it in view and aim at it; the broad gully up to the pass is right there. If you have run out of the rising traverse without a blocky tower above you, you are low and short of the pass.

The climbing itself starts at High Pass, where you cross onto the glacier. Snow travel of up to about thirty-five degrees leads to the summit snow ridge. The final marker is at the very top: by midsummer the bergschrund and moat below the summit rock often force a short section of fifth-class rock or a delicate roped step across a snow bridge, so the route does not simply walk out on snow.
hazards: barricaded Moose Creek bridge at the start
avalanche terrain in the entry couloir to Lone Tree Pass
vague, brushy route-finding with deadfall above 'the flat'
crevasses on the Whitehorse Glacier from roughly July onward
summit bergschrund and moat, often a fifth-class or roped step by midsummer
no reliable water once you are on snow

approach_variants.name: Snow Gulch direct (deep snow only)
approach_variants.season: early season, deep snow burying the brush
approach_variants.notes: A more direct line used by some early-season and ski parties. From the Niederprum trailhead area, follow the old forest-road grade toward Snow Gulch, then ascend the creek drainage. The section between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft is a steep bushwhack through slide alder or up the adjacent slabs, and it only makes sense once deep snow has buried the brush. Parties commonly stash skis or boards around 2,500 ft in the old growth for the descent.
approach_variants.baseFinding: This variation rejoins the same upper ground, so the markers are unchanged: White Benchmark (Point 6357) for the traverse to High Pass, and High Pass itself as the step onto the glacier. The specific trap here is timing rather than terrain — if you are fighting slide alder rather than walking on snow, the line is out of condition and the standard Niederprum trail is the better choice that day.
hazards: slide alder and slabs between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft when snow cover is thin
avalanche hazard in the gulch and on the glacier headwall in the early-season window

approach_variants.name: Tupso Pass trailhead, Trail #641 (road drivable)
approach_variants.notes:
Trail #641 from the Tupso Pass trailhead at the end of FR 41. Forest to Saddle Lake at about two and a half miles — the last easy water, with no fires and no camping within two hundred feet of the shore beyond this point — then up through meadows to Goat Flats at roughly four and a half miles, which has the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound.

From Goat Flats the trail climbs about two more miles to Tin Can Gap at roughly six miles, banking most of the day's gain. That is the effective end of the maintained trail and where most walkers turn back.

The trail has been maintained by volunteers in recent years, with large numbers of logs cleared; note that a big fallen log above Saddle Lake has rerouted the tread, and there is a rough connector going straight up and down to the next switchback.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Past Tin Can Gap you drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb Glacier. Late in the season you can avoid the ice entirely by staying in the MOAT between the top edge of the glacier and the rock — and finding the entrance to that moat is the thing that goes wrong in bad weather. The trail crosses back to the north side of the ridge shortly before it and you meet the top of the glacier there; if you are on the south side of the ridge you have not crossed over yet.

The start of the actual climbing is not in doubt once you can see it: three wooden ladders, stacked in sequence and pinned into the rock with rebar and steel cable, run up the final rock band to the lookout deck. There is nothing else like them on the mountain. The transition between the second and third ladder is the hardest move and is awkward with a full pack, and the exposure is real.

The negative marker is which summit you are on. The lookout — and therefore the ladders — is on the SOUTH peak. If you have crossed the glacier and are scrambling rock toward a col with no ladders anywhere in view, you are heading for the Middle or North peak instead. Some parties also report a hand-line on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier; treat any fixed rope there as unverified.
hazards: moat between glacier and rock that widens through the season and is hard to enter in poor visibility
crevasses on the Queest-Alb once it opens up
exposure on the ladders, particularly between the second and third
unverified fixed hand-line on the rock step past Tin Can Gap

approach_variants.name: Road-closure variation — walk or bike FR 41
approach_variants.season: whenever the road is closed at the washout
approach_variants.notes:
FR 41 has washed out repeatedly and the closure point has moved. Reported blockages have been around five miles up from the Mountain Loop Highway, and at other times past the Canyon Creek bridge, leaving roughly nine miles of road between the closure and the trailhead. Vehicles are barred past the barrier but foot and bike traffic are allowed, and biking the road is the common tactic.

Treat this as a standing possibility rather than a one-off: check with the Darrington Ranger District or the Verlot Public Service Center before committing, because the difference is a day hike versus an overnight. There is now a sign at the road marking the old trailhead.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Once you reach Tupso Pass the route is identical, and the same markers apply: cross to the north side of the ridge past Tin Can Gap to meet the top of the Queest-Alb, find the moat entrance rather than stepping onto open ice, and finish on the three stacked ladders on the SOUTH peak.
hazards: several miles of road walking or biking each way with the resulting late finish
all the hazards of the standard variation once on trail

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 to White Pass and Glacier Gap
approach_variants.notes:
North Fork Sauk River trailhead at about 2,050 ft, off Sloan Creek Road (FR 49). The trail runs gently through old growth: the Pilot Ridge junction at roughly two miles, a crossing of Red Creek at about three and a half that can be a real obstacle early in the season, and Mackinaw Shelter about a mile and a half further — the last flat camping with easy water before the climb steepens.

Past the shelter the trail switchbacks hard for about three miles and two thousand feet to meet the Pacific Crest Trail; turn right and go a quarter mile to White Pass at about 5,900 ft. This is the standard high-camp area and the end of maintained trail.

From White Pass a use trail traverses north into the White Chuck Glacier basin. Skirt or cross the glacier and rise onto its north-east lobe to Glacier Gap at about 7,250 ft.

This has become the main way up Glacier Peak since the White Chuck trail on the west side washed out, and it makes for a round trip in the mid-thirties of miles — considerably longer than the historic approach.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Glacier Gap is the reference point and it has a definition you can verify in cloud: it is the col where the White Chuck and the Suiattle glaciers MEET. If you are standing on a saddle with ice on only one side of you, it is not Glacier Gap.

Above the gap the cleaver begins as a gentle ridge and sharpens as it runs north. That gentleness is why parties overshoot the start — there is no abrupt step to tell you the route has begun. From here there are two choices, and they are genuinely different climbs: go directly over Disappointment Peak, which is fourth class, or skirt it by climbing the upper margins of the Gerdine and Cool glaciers.

The negative marker that matters most on this route is near the top. The first summit reached along the cleaver is Disappointment Peak, not Glacier Peak — if you have topped out and the true summit is still rising well above and beyond you across more ground, you are on Disappointment and have not finished.

One more, on the way in: the traverse from White Pass toward the Cool Glacier passes below Disappointment Peak's east face, which is a rockfall corridor. Helmets on, and stay higher and further out from the base of the peak rather than hugging it.
hazards: Red Creek ford early in the season
rockfall corridor below Disappointment Peak's east face on the traverse in
crevasses on the White Chuck, Gerdine and Cool glaciers
fourth-class ground if the direct line over Disappointment Peak is taken
long committing round trip well into the thirties of miles

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then the Foam Creek high traverse
approach_variants.notes:
From the North Fork Sauk River trailhead at about 2,050 ft, take Trail #649 up the valley and then the steep switchbacks to the Pacific Crest Trail at White Pass, roughly nine miles in.

Rather than dropping into the basin, continue east on the Foam Creek trail for about two miles, cross a ridge saddle near 6,600 ft, and traverse the White Chuck Glacier basin trending north-east to Glacier Gap at about 7,250 ft — where the Suiattle and White Chuck glaciers meet, and the standard high camp.

Summit day from Glacier Gap is short in distance but has intermediate descent in it as well as gain: gentle snow above camp, then a climbers' track over volcanic scree onto the Gerdine and Cool glaciers.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Glacier Gap is confirmed the same way as for the cleaver — it is the col where two glaciers meet, not a saddle with ice on one side only.

This route deliberately AVOIDS the fourth-class ground: the line skirts Disappointment Peak by staying on the upper edges of the Gerdine and then the Cool. So the test that you are on the right variation is that you are on snow and scree the whole way, working around the peak rather than over it. If you are scrambling rock and gaining a summit, you have drifted onto the direct line over Disappointment Peak.

On the Cool Glacier expect to end-run one or two crevasses before rejoining the climbers' track for the final steep pitch to the summit — that track, worn into scree and snow by traffic, is the most reliable confirmation you are on the standard line, so look for it rather than for a feature.
hazards: rockfall corridor below Disappointment Peak on the traverse
crevasses on the Gerdine and Cool glaciers
loose volcanic scree on the connecting ground
long approach with no maintained trail above White Pass

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River Trail #643 (the historic standard)
approach_variants.notes:
This was the standard way up Glacier Peak and the road access has been unreliable for a very long time. The last several miles of FR 23 to the White Chuck trailhead have been reported blocked — at one point with large boulders placed at the turnoff — and reports of the road being driveable and undriveable have alternated over the years. Confirm with the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie forest before relying on it, because in a bad year the effective trailhead moves miles downstream.

From the trailhead at about 2,350 ft the trail runs upstream through old growth, crossing Pumice, Glacier and Kennedy Creeks — reliable water, but high with snowmelt in early summer. At about five and a half miles is the old Kennedy Hot Springs area at around 3,300 ft, still a popular campsite; the pool, lodge and guard station were destroyed by the 2003 flood and never rebuilt, so there is no usable hot pool there.

Another mile and a half brings you to Sitkum Creek and the PCT junction at about 3,850 ft. Turn north on the PCT for about half a mile to a forested camp near 4,100 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The path that leaves the PCT for Boulder Basin is unsigned and steeper than anything before it — climbers describe it as more of a fisherman's track than a trail. The test is direction, not appearance: the correct path goes STRAIGHT UP the forested ridge. Anything that contours is the PCT or a game trail.

You know you have arrived at the top of it when the trees break: Boulder Basin at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft is heather and rock benches with running water, and it is the standard high camp. If you are still in continuous forest, you are below it, however long the climb has felt.

From camp the route ascends snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum. Rope up at the point the snowfield stops being a slope you can see the bottom of and becomes continuous glacier — there is no rock landmark for this, so the transition is judged on the ground rather than found.
hazards: unreliable road access to the trailhead over many years
creek fords running high with early-summer snowmelt
steep unmaintained climbers' path with no signage leaving the PCT
crevasses on the Sitkum

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk and the PCT (the reliable alternative)
approach_variants.notes: Because the White Chuck side has been unreliable for years, parties reach this side of the mountain instead from the North Fork Sauk River trailhead, climbing to White Pass on the PCT and then travelling north over Red Pass toward the Glacier Creek and Sitkum ground. It is substantially longer and is chosen for access rather than for the climbing.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route above is unchanged: the marker is Boulder Basin — trees giving way to heather and rock benches with running water at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft — and then snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum above it. Arriving from the north on the PCT the risk is passing the drainage entirely, so identify the Sitkum Creek and Glacier Creek junctions on the map before you set out rather than expecting signage.
hazards: very long approach on the PCT with substantial gain and loss
no signed junction for the climbers' path

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the 7,200 ft camp
approach_variants.notes:
White Chuck River trailhead at about 2,300 ft — subject to the same long-running road access problems as the Sitkum approach, so confirm before relying on it. Follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about six miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail about a mile and three quarters to the PCT.

Head north on the PCT about three miles — roughly two thirds of a mile past the Kennedy Creek crossing, which is your water — to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the trail. That path climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The high camp at about 7,200 ft on snow and pumice is the staging point, not the route. From there the approach continues across the upper south-west slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to a saddle at 8,000 ft between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers, then up the Kennedy Glacier — loose moraine and boulders low down — to a saddle at about 8,800 ft. THAT saddle is where Frostbite Ridge proper begins, and it is the last bivy site before the crater.

The critical navigation warning is about the Rabbit Ears. They are the route's famous feature, a pair of eroded lava pinnacles, and they are NOT visible until you are immediately below them, slightly east of the ridge crest. Do not try to navigate toward them from a distance and do not conclude you are off route because you cannot see them — get to the 8,800 ft saddle and follow the crest, and they will appear.

Above the Ears the ridge steepens into alpine ice, reported anywhere from a single short step to a couple of hundred feet, before the crater rim.
hazards: long-running road access problems on the White Chuck side
unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT
loose moraine and boulders low on the Kennedy Glacier
very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers

approach_variants.name: Suiattle River Road and the PCT via Milk Creek
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) from Darrington to its end at Sulphur Creek Campground. Follow the Suiattle River trail about seven miles to the bridge over the river, then the PCT southbound about nine miles to a camp in the East Fork Milk Creek basin at about 5,600 ft. From there continue up the ridge on snow and pumice to the same standard high camp near 7,200 ft.

The Suiattle River Road has a long history of flood damage and multi-year closures, so its status is worth confirming rather than assuming.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical above the 7,200 ft camp: traverse the upper south-west Ptarmigan slopes to about 8,000 ft, round Kennedy Peak to the 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers, up the Kennedy to the 8,800 ft saddle where the ridge begins. Remember that the Rabbit Ears stay hidden until you are directly beneath them slightly east of the crest.
hazards: repeated flood damage and long closures on the Suiattle River Road
very long PCT approach day
same upper-mountain hazards as the Kennedy Ridge variation

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then north
approach_variants.notes: Some parties use the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass — about nine miles and 5,900 ft — and then make a long traverse north on or near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area. It is a twenty-mile-plus approach day and is chosen when the other two roads are out.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same as the other variations: the 8,800 ft saddle above the Kennedy Glacier is where the ridge starts, and the Rabbit Ears do not become visible until you are immediately below them.
hazards: twenty-mile-plus approach day
same upper-mountain hazards as the other variations

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek route
approach_variants.notes:
From the Suiattle River Road, take the Downey Creek Trail on the east bank through old growth — about six and a half miles to the Six Mile campsite at roughly 2,440 ft. The maintained trail effectively ends there.

The Bachelor Creek route continues on the north side of the creek and crosses to the south at about 4,000 ft on a log; some parties cross higher, nearer 4,400. Between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft the tread is genuinely overgrown — parties describe swimming through brush without being able to see their feet — but the important point is that the trail IS still there under it, so do not abandon it and start making your own line. At about 4,500 ft an old avalanche swath from 2002 wiped out the trail and this is the hardest stretch to get through.

Above that, cross the pass at about 5,900 ft north-west of Cub Lake and descend to the lake at 5,338 ft, around fourteen miles in. Good camping. A well-established trail then crosses flats and climbs heather beside a cascade to Itswoot Ridge at about 6,200 ft, which is the better-placed camp for summit day. Reported car-to-camp times have been nine to eleven hours; this is a multi-day approach, not a hike-in.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Itswoot Ridge the traverse north-east toward the Dome Glacier goes through a basin that is well marked with CAIRNS and is followable even with reduced visibility — so in cloud, look for cairns rather than trying to hold a bearing. Losing the cairns is the sign you have drifted.

The climbing starts where you rope up at the glacier's edge. The upper Dome Glacier is mellow, so the arrival is undramatic; the feature you are climbing to is the notch or col at 8,560 ft immediately NORTH of the summit block. It is confirmed by what happens on the far side: from the col a snow slope of about three hundred feet and then a rock arete of about five hundred feet lead to the summit at 8,920 ft.

The useful cross-check in poor visibility is that the col also gives onto the Chickamin Glacier beyond — a much larger icefield than the one you came up. So a very big glacier appearing on the far side is CORRECT and not a sign you are in the wrong place; the thing to verify is that the summit block is immediately to your south. If the ground on the far side does not drop away onto a large icefield, you are at a different notch.
hazards: brush so dense between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft that the trail is invisible underfoot
the 2002 avalanche swath at about 4,500 ft where the trail is destroyed
Bachelor Creek crossing on a log
open avalanche paths below Spire Point in early-season snow
crevasses on the Dome Glacier
unmarked cross-country traverse if the cairns are lost

approach_variants.name: Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass
approach_variants.notes: Dome Peak is the far end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, so it is also reached from the Cascade Pass trailhead by travelling the whole traverse south. This is the long way in by a wide margin and is undertaken as part of the traverse rather than as an approach to the peak; parties heading only for Dome use the Downey Creek side.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Arriving from the north along the traverse, the reference points are the same: the cairned basin traverse toward the Dome Glacier, and the 8,560 ft col north of the summit block with the Chickamin Glacier beyond it and the summit rock arete immediately to the south.
hazards: multi-day committing traverse with several glacier crossings before Dome is reached
crevasses on the Dome Glacier

approach_variants.name: Holden Village via the Lake Chelan ferry, then Holden Lake and Holden Pass
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct, best early to mid July
approach_variants.notes:
Getting to the trailhead is part of the trip and it runs on someone else's timetable: drive to Chelan, take the Lady of the Lake ferry up the lake to the Lucerne landing, then the roughly thirteen-mile bus up to Holden Village at about 3,300 ft. Reservations and a look at the ferry and bus schedules come before anything else in the planning.

From Holden, walk the gravel road and Railroad Creek Trail west about a mile to the signed Holden Lake Trail junction and bear right. That trail climbs steadily about four miles through forest and brush, with small side-creek crossings for water, to Holden Lake at 5,278 ft, in a cirque directly beneath Bonanza's east face — a natural camp and the last easy water.

Past the lake outlet the tread fades. Skirt the north shore through slide alder and talus, which is real bushwhacking and route-finding especially with high water early in the season, then climb a hillside traverse north-west to Holden Pass at 6,360 ft — the standard high camp and the last reliable water before the glacier. That is roughly five miles and three thousand feet from the village.

It is worth going in July in most years: later the glacier breaks up and the problem becomes getting off the ice and onto the rock at all.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Holden Pass a use trail — which may be under snow — climbs north and west toward the ridge. After several hundred feet of gain you reach a large ledge at about 6,700 ft, often snow-covered. That ledge is the first checkpoint; if you are still on the pass or on undifferentiated slope, you have not gained it.

The unmistakable marker for the start of the climbing is water. Above the ledge is a set of low-angle slabs with a waterfall running down them, draining the Mary Green Glacier — the 'waterfall slabs'. Running water on slabby rock at around 7,000 to 7,300 ft is the confirmation you are in the right place; there is nothing else like it on this side of the peak.

The route up them is class 3 and the rule is to start HIGH and to the RIGHT, skirting the waterfall rather than climbing through it. That is the test that separates the right line from the wrong one: if water is running over the rock you are on, and the holds are wet and mossy, you are too far left and too low — traverse right and up before committing. Topping the slabs puts you on the northern edge of the glacier.

On the glacier itself, bear west along its north (climber's right) edge, then traverse south-west along the base of the north-east ridge to the glacier's upper corner, where the moat is usually a single step across onto rock.
hazards: wet, slabby class 3 with a waterfall running through it below the glacier
loose, rockfall-prone gullies below the glacier's retreating margin — keep out of the fall line of parties above
icefall above the slabs
moat at the top of the glacier, which widens through the season
slide alder and vague route-finding past Holden Lake, worst with high water
black flies between about 3,000 and 4,000 ft, mosquitoes from the lake upward
the trip is gated by the ferry and bus schedule, so a delay is not recoverable on the day

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass and the Ptarmigan Traverse to the Spider-Formidable col
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade Pass trailhead at 3,600 ft at the end of the Cascade River Road. The maintained trail runs 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft — well graded, an hour and a half to two hours at a steady pace. Everything beyond is bootpath and it is the start of the Ptarmigan Traverse.

From the pass take the bootpath uphill to the south and traverse along Mix-Up Arm on heather, talus and snow, then up the mellow Cache Glacier to Cache Col at about 6,900 ft — corniced early in the season. From the col, a descending traverse south-south-east on more heather, talus and snow reaches Kool-Aid Lake at 6,100 ft, the standard base camp, roughly three hours and five to six miles from Cascade Pass.

South past Art's Knoll comes the Red Ledge: an exposed traverse over loose rock and lingering snow patches that many parties rope for, and by common consent the crux of the approach. It is noticeably worse when snow-covered.

Beyond it a rough path runs about a mile over meadow, snow, talus and small rock ribs toward the Middle Cascade Glacier icefall at around 6,500 ft. Rope up, ascend the glacier's left side weaving through crevasses, and reach the Spider-Formidable col at 7,320 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the part that is easy to get wrong, and it is a counting exercise rather than a description.

From the col, go through the NARROW EASTERN notch and descend roughly 150 vertical feet of steep snow — or in the moat beside it — before it becomes feasible to start contouring right, to the west. Do not try to contour immediately from the notch; you have to lose that height first.

Continue west over slabs and snow, then heather and small rock outcrops. Leave the snow onto class 3 rock, climb up and then LEFT to a distinct ledge. From that ledge make a rising traverse to the north-west, scrambling ACROSS two gullies. Then cross a spur ridge to reach a THIRD gully — and it is the third gully that you climb.

So the test is: from the ledge, the first two gullies are crossed, not entered. If you start up the first gully you meet after the ledge you will be on steeper, looser ground short of the line. If you have crossed a spur ridge and are looking up a gully, that is the one.

Some trip reports also describe reaching the south-face snow alcove from a staging camp near a notch at about 7,050 ft below the col, by either a hidden gully on the left with fifth-class moves or, more commonly, a winding ledge on the right at class 3 with one harder step. The right-hand ledge is the usual choice; if you are pulling fifth-class moves you have taken the left option.
hazards: the Red Ledge — loose rock, exposed, and materially worse when snow-covered
cornice at Cache Col early in the season
crevasses on the Middle Cascade Glacier icefall
steep snow and moat immediately below the Spider-Formidable notch
loose rock in the gullies on the south face
long, remote position with no maintained trail beyond Cascade Pass

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass and the Ptarmigan Traverse
approach_variants.notes:
Formidable sits deep on the Ptarmigan Traverse and is reached the same way as the south side: Cascade Pass trailhead at 3,600 ft, 3.7 miles of maintained trail to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then bootpath only.

From the pass, traverse south along Mix-Up Arm on heather, talus and snow, ascend the Cache Glacier to Cache Col at about 6,900 ft (corniced early), and make a descending traverse south-south-east to Kool-Aid Lake at 6,100 ft. South of there the Red Ledge is the crux of the walking — exposed, loose, and worse under snow — and beyond it a rough path leads about a mile to the Middle Cascade Glacier.

Parties on the north side of the peak generally camp further along the traverse, near Yang Yang Lakes, and work back up toward the mountain from there. This is a full multi-day mountaineering trip with no maintained trail after Cascade Pass, normally done as part of the traverse rather than as a there-and-back.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The reliable checkpoints on the way in are all named ground rather than route features: Cache Col (a glacier col, corniced early season), Kool-Aid Lake (a small meltwater tarn — the standard camp, and the last obvious flat ground for a while), the Red Ledge (the only place on the traverse where you are moving across loose rock on an exposed shelf and thinking about a rope), and the Spider-Formidable col at 7,320 ft, reached by roping up the Middle Cascade Glacier's icefall.

Be clear which side of the mountain you are aiming for before you leave camp, because the traverse passes both. The commonly climbed line from this ground is the south side, reached by descending east of the col and traversing west; a north-side line is a different objective on the far flank of the peak. No source consulted gave a specific, verifiable description of where the north-side climbing starts, so that last stretch is not recorded here rather than guessed at.
hazards: the Red Ledge — loose rock on an exposed shelf, worse when snow-covered
cornice at Cache Col early season
crevasses on the Cache and Middle Cascade glaciers
multi-day committing position with no maintained trail past Cascade Pass
